newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE-Convicted Italian killer pleads "enzyme effect".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Convicted Italian killer pleads "enzyme effect".

text.p: An Italian sentenced to 17 years in jail for murder will argue at an appeal that opened on Thursday that a temporary enzyme imbalance triggered a killer impulse, newspapers reported.
They said it was the first time such a defence had been argued in an Italian court.

Angelo Ortolina, a 41-year-old primary school teacher, was found guilty of premeditated murder over the shooting of his lover Antonia Magni in May 1995. They had argued when he told her he wanted to leave her.

Italian newspapers said lawyers for Ortolina intended to cite scientific evidence that at the time their client had excessive levels in his blood of creatine kinase or CPK, an enzyme found in some muscular tissue including the heart.

"CPK could be the trigger for a transitory psychiatric illness, determined in this case by the pressure the victim applied against Ortolina's desire to end their relationship," Corriere della Sera quoted one of the man's lawyers as saying.
The lawyer, Gugliemo Gulotta, an expert in criminal psychiatry, said the defence team wanted the appeal court to agree to a scientific study of the case as a prelude to a review of the conviction.
Gulotta was not available for comment. His office confirmed the appeal hearing was under way before a court in Milan.
Ortolina's CPK levels were measured during medical tests he was having at the time of the shooting but were not cited as evidence at his trial.
La Repubblica quoted a scientist unconnected with the case as saying the defence broke new ground in forensic psychiatry though he did not believe the enzyme triggered violence.
"Creatine kinase is released by the organism each time there is very intense muscular activity," psychiatrist Enrico Smeraldi said.
"It is present in great quantities in the organism of athletes who have undergone particularly tiring training but that does not mean they become dangerously aggressive," he said.
